abstract: This Penn Wharton Budget Model analysis projects that generative AI will increase productivity and GDP by 1.5% by 2035, nearly 3% by 2055, and 3.7% by 2075. The study estimates that 40% of current labor income is exposed to AI automation, with peak productivity growth contributions occurring in the early 2030s at 0.2 percentage points before gradually declining as adoption saturates. Task-level cost savings average 25% from current AI tools and could reach 40% as systems improve, though the permanent long-term boost to growth is modest at less than 0.04 percentage points.
keyFindings: Approximately 40 percent of current GDP could be substantially affected by generative AI, with occupations around the 80th percentile of earnings most exposed, averaging about 50 percent of work susceptible to automation.

AI's contribution to total factor productivity growth will peak in 2032 at around 0.2 percentage points before declining, with a permanent effect of less than 0.04 percentage points after adoption saturates.

Current generative AI tools deliver average labor cost savings of approximately 25 percent, with potential to reach 40 percent as systems improve, based on studies showing gains ranging from 10 to 55 percent across various applications.

Employment in occupations with 100 percent AI automation potential fell 0.75 percent from 2021 to 2024, while growth slowed significantly in high-exposure occupations (90-99 percent automatable) since 2022.

Generative AI adoption at work reached 26.4 percent of workers in the second half of 2024, with adoption patterns broadly similar to personal computer adoption in the early 1980s, suggesting full workplace integration within 15 years.
methodology: Task-based framework combining Acemoglu (2024) model with AI exposure estimates from Eloundou et al. (2024) applied to 784 detailed occupational categories. Employment and wage data from Bureau of Labor Statistics Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics (OEWS) for 2021-2024. Adoption timeline based on Real-Time Population Survey (RPS) data for generative AI combined with historical diffusion patterns of personal computers, internet, cloud computing, and smartphones. Cost savings estimates derived from meta-analysis of seven recent empirical studies of AI adoption outcomes. GDP impact projections calculated using formula: long-run TFP change = GDP share of exposed tasks × percentage cost savings × adoption rate.
qualifiers: Authors note that caution is required interpreting these projections based on limited data on AI's initial effects. Analysis does not account for AI-driven changes in product quality, emergence of new products and labor tasks, or potential feedback effects on innovation. Exposure estimates are based on task-level automation potential thresholds (jobs with at least 50 percent of tasks automatable are classified as exposed) which may not reflect actual profitability or feasibility of automation. Only 23 percent of exposed tasks assumed to be eventually automated based on Svanberg et al. (2024) findings. Projections are preliminary and subject to significant revision as more data becomes available. US-only analysis. Employment changes presented in Figure 4 are described as suggestive evidence rather than definitive proof of AI impact.
